https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: A purple patch on my voyage of discovery
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Pace of change and knowledge development are so rapid within the natural world that nature writings can quickly go out of date. There are also rebel species that loathe being imprisoned within empirical boxes, none more so than our haughty purple emperor butterfly.
So, having published what some (but not me) may regard as a definitive treatise on this recalcitrant insect, I find a significant revision is due — not because I got something badly wrong (that nightmare may yet arise) — but because a breakthrough has occurred in an area formerly closed to study. A set of traffic lights stuck interminably at red has suddenly turned green.
The insect spends three weeks in the pupal period, suspended from a leaf in the upper regions of a tree — safe from study though, as I found, not safe from predation — turning from biochemical soup into a winged butterfly through the miraculous final stage of its metamorphosis.
It has recently been discovered that purple emperor pupae fluoresce, or glow prominently in the dark under the beam of a powerful UV torch (itself a newish development). This is part of a bigger discovery that has opened another great area of research; it has been found that the larvae of several of our more elusive butterflies fluoresce, and can be found with relative ease by night with the right piece of equipment. Sadly, purple emperor larvae do not fluoresce. That would have been too much to ask.
All this means that some scientifically minded butterfly enthusiasts have been wandering the midnight woods with UV torches, discovering new colonies of some of our more elusive species, pushing back the frontiers of knowledge. About 30 pupae of the purple emperor have been found, as far afield as Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire, woods in West Sussex and near Savernake Forest in Wiltshire. By emperor standards that’s a massive sample.
Unfortunately, most of these pupae vanished without trace, predated by creatures unknown. That fits with my previous, rather meagre, studies of this crucial life stage. The next task, of course, is to erect trail cameras close to the cryptic pupae, a job for next year. The main culprit may be larger birds, if they can see within the UV range, but also the nocturnal hazel dormouse, wood mouse or yellow-necked mouse. Some of our scarcer tree bats, Bechstein’s and Natterer’s, which practise quiet echo-location and can glean off foliage, may also be involved.
Yet another voyage of discovery is under way. Butterflying, and “emperoring”, just got even better.
Extinction rebellionIn 2000 a species of bee-fly that looks and behaves like a small golden-haired hoverfly flew gloriously into my life. The textbook British Soldierflies and their Allies suggested it had been extinct here for several decades, though I soon found out that a colony had just been rediscovered in the southern Chilterns. Nonetheless, my discovery of a sizeable colony in the Cotswolds was significant. Since then, Villa cingulata or the downland bee-fly as it has become known, has been found over much of central southern England, notably in the home counties and on the Cotswold grasslands, where it is relatively numerous. It’s a species on the up at a time of unprecedented biodiversity loss, a welcome good news story.
I’d like to be able to say that its ecology is well understood but entomologists are so busy revelling in the joy of turning it up in new localities that its precise needs have yet to be clarified. The assumption, and we must be wary of assumptions in the natural world, is that its larvae are parasites of those of moths or mining bees. All will become clear. It is unlikely to become a problem or pest species.
This week I was part of a group of naturalists who discovered the downland bee-fly in some numbers on the rewilding site at Knepp Castle Estate in West Sussex. The females were busy gathering particles of dust with which to make their eggs heavier, apparently, so they can fire weighted eggs into their hosts’ hiding places — precision bombing, insect-style.
Wildly successfulEach year some species of wildflower fare particularly well and claim the year as theirs. Lady’s bedstraw turned many a road verge soft-yellow last year. My plant of 2021 is actually two closely related species that produce yellow flowers in early summer: creeping cinquefoil and silverweed. Google the former and you’ll read how to eliminate this pernicious weed from your lawn. Both benefited from last summer’s droughts, as colonisers of bare ground. Both have their associated insects.
Matthew Oates’s His Imperial Majesty, a natural history of the purple emperor butterfly, is available in paperback
